passage:
I'm Lalremsiami, and for a long time I counted the moments I missed. Shalini's first steps happened while I was at a quarterly audit, and I heard about them on a video call. I kept a list of guilt in my head. It didn't shorten my working day; it only made me sour at home.

The change came when I chose three times when my phone goes in a drawer: breakfast, the Wednesday walk to the park after school, and bedtime stories on Saturday. In those hours I'm completely there. Shalini doesn't know how long I work, but she knows Wednesday is ours.

I still ache sometimes. But I've stopped punishing myself for a life with real trade-offs, and I try to be present where I can.

qa.q: When does Lalremsiami put the phone in a drawer?
qa.a: At breakfast, on the Wednesday walk to the park after school, and at bedtime stories on Saturday.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami's guilt make things worse at first?
qa.a: The guilt didn't shorten the working day; it only made Lalremsiami sour at home.
Choosing a few protected times of full attention with the phone in a drawer, and accepting the real trade-offs of the working life.

qa.q: What might Shalini take from the Wednesday walks?
qa.a: Shalini may not know how long Lalremsiami works, but knows Wednesday is theirs together, which gives Shalini something steady to count on.

grounding: A working parent guilty about missed moments protects a few times of full attention and forgives a life with real trade-offs.

passage:
Pradeep, you think you are the first parent to miss things for work? Sit down. Your Vasudha paati was a doctor, remember.

When your mother was small, I did night duty at the government hospital three times a week. I missed her first steps. I missed her school play; she was a tree. I would come home at seven in the morning and she'd be asleep, and I would stand at her bed feeling like a thief who had stolen her own child's days.

For two years I lived in that guilt, and it made me snappy and tired on the days I was home.

Then I made two promises. Every Sunday breakfast was ours, dosas and no hospital calls. And on nights off, I read to her, one chapter, no matter how tired. That's all.

You can't be everywhere, kanna. Be completely there when you are. And forgive yourself for the rest.

qa.q: What part did Pradeep's mother play in the school play?
How did young Vasudha feel standing at her daughter's bed after night duty?
qa.a: She felt guilty, like a thief who had stolen her own child's days.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vasudha's story?
qa.a: She chose two protected times, Sunday breakfasts and bedtime reading on nights off, and gave them her full attention.

qa.q: How might Vasudha's daughter have felt about the Sunday dosas?
qa.a: She probably felt loved and looked forward to them, knowing her mother was fully hers then.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young mother working long hours and guilty about missing her child's moments, who chooses protected times of full attention and forgives herself.

passage:
The flight from Hyderabad was delayed by three hours, and Sumit sat at the gate watching the minutes of Lokesh's annual day go by on his phone. His son, five, was a sunflower. Sumit had promised.

He felt sick. This was the third event this year. He ran a small logistics firm, and when a truck broke down, the phone didn't care who was dancing.

His wife sent a video: Lokesh on stage, searching the crowd, then waving at her. Sumit watched it four times.

He landed at eleven. Lokesh was asleep. Sumit sat on the bed in the dark.

The next morning he made two decisions and wrote them on the fridge whiteboard. Every Sunday morning: cycling with Papa, phone in the drawer. Every Wednesday: Papa does bedtime.

"Sorry I missed it, beta. Show me your sunflower dance?" Lokesh danced it in the kitchen, twice, in his pyjamas. Sumit clapped like the whole audience.

qa.q: What was Lokesh at the annual day?
What was Sumit feeling as he watched the video at the gate?
qa.a: Sumit felt sick with guilt at missing another of his son's events.

qa.q: What did Sumit decide, and why is it a good approach?
qa.a: He set protected times, Sunday cycling with his phone put away and Wednesday bedtimes, so his son gets full attention even in a busy life.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt dancing for his father in the kitchen?
qa.a: Lokesh likely felt happy and seen, getting his own private show for Papa.

grounding: The story shows a young father who works long hours and feels guilty about missing his child's events, choosing protected times of full attention and forgiving himself.
